purpose: Repository Corticotropin is used to treat a variety of conditions including flare-ups of multiple sclerosis, certain kidney problems (like nephrotic syndrome), severe allergic reactions, and some inflammatory conditions. It is also used to treat infantile spasms, a rare type of seizure disorder in babies. Doctors may prescribe it when other treatments have not worked well enough.
how_it_works: This medication works by stimulating your adrenal glands, which sit on top of your kidneys, to produce natural steroids like cortisol. These natural steroids help calm down inflammation and overactive immune responses in your body. Think of it as sending a signal to your body to make its own powerful anti-inflammatory substances.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention or swelling, mood changes or trouble sleeping, increased blood sugar levels, higher blood pressure, and increased risk of infections. You may also notice stomach upset or skin changes like acne.
warnings: This medication can weaken your immune system, making it harder to fight infections, so avoid contact with people who are sick. Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor, as your body needs time to adjust. It can raise blood sugar levels, so people with diabetes need to monitor their levels carefully. Tell your doctor if you have any infections, history of stomach ulcers, heart problems, or mental health conditions before starting this medication.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an injection under the skin or into the muscle, and is not taken by mouth. The dose depends on your condition and weight (especially in children). For adults with MS flares, a common dose is 80 to 120 units per day for 2 to 3 weeks. Your doctor or nurse will teach you or a caregiver how to give the injection at home if needed. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your situation.
